draft.title: Royal debt and financial crisis
card: By the 1780s the French crown spent much more than it earned. It had borrowed heavily to cover the gap.
Wars were the main cause of the debt. France fought several costly wars in the 1700s, including the Seven Years' War, which it lost.
France also helped the American colonists against Britain, with money, supplies, soldiers and a navy. This war added a very large sum to the debt.
Much of the crown's income then went to paying interest on past loans. The crown was close to bankruptcy, which meant it needed new ways to raise money.
draft.remember: Costly wars, including aid to America, left the crown close to bankruptcy.

a.q: Which statement best explains why the French crown was close to bankruptcy in the 1780s?
opts: It had borrowed to pay for costly wars and owed interest
It had spent its savings on rebuilding Paris after a fire
It had lost most of its tax income when the colonies left
It had paid huge sums to Britain after winning a war
a.why: The card says wars were the main cause, and the crown borrowed to fund them. The interest on those loans then took much of its income. Losing tax income because colonies left is a tempting mistake, but the card gives no such cause.
a.clue: Think about how the crown paid for its wars.

b.q: Marc's family farm borrows money each year to cover costs. Soon most of their income goes to paying interest. How is this like the French crown in the 1780s?
opts: Past loans took much of the crown's income as interest
The crown had no loans but spent its savings on war
The crown paid off its loans by taxing the nobles
The crown's income fell because trade with America stopped
b.why: Like Marc's family, the crown had borrowed heavily, so a large share of its income went to interest on old loans. The crown was not paying off its debts by taxing the nobles, so that option is wrong.
b.clue: Look at what happens to income once old loans pile up.

a.best: It had borrowed to pay for costly wars and owed interest

b.best: Past loans took much of the crown's income as interest

problems.detail: The stem describes borrowing and income going to interest, and the right option is the only one that mentions interest or income going to past loans. A student can match the words without knowing the French case.

a.q: Which statement best explains why the French crown was close to bankruptcy in the 1780s?
opts: It had borrowed to pay for costly wars and owed interest
It had spent most of its income on royal palaces and feasts
It had spent its savings on rebuilding Paris after a fire
It had paid huge sums to Britain after winning a war
a.why: Wars were the main cause of the debt, and the crown borrowed to fund them. The interest on those loans then took much of its income. Court spending on palaces is a common belief, but the card names wars as the main cause.
a.clue: Think about how the crown paid for its wars.

b.q: A student says France's help to the American colonists gave it glory at little cost. What is the best reply?
opts: The aid added a very large sum to an already heavy debt
The aid was cheap, as France sent only money and supplies
The aid cost little, as Britain repaid France after the war
The aid mattered little, as France had no debts before it
b.why: France sent money, supplies, soldiers and a navy, and this war added a very large sum to a debt already built up by earlier wars. The claim that France sent only money and supplies is tempting, but France also sent soldiers and a navy.
b.clue: Recall what France sent and what the war did to the debt.

a.best: It had borrowed to pay for costly wars and owed interest

b.best: The aid added a very large sum to an already heavy debt
